Posted May 23, 2002
Analysis by Richard Cowan
(MarijuanaNews note: On Monday, May 13th, Canada’s Global National News with Kevin Newman began with a story about how the DEAland prohibitionists were threatening Canadian sovereignty by insisting that Canadian cannabis polices mirror those of its southern neighbor.

The interview with Robert Maginnis, of the Family Research Council, hit a raw nerve even with Canadians who were not particularly anti-prohibitionist.

So it was all the more surprising when on May 17th the National Post, one of Canada’s two national newspapers, owned by the same media company as Global, ran an article by the same reporters, entitled " U.S. fears drug spillover from Canada -- Border seizures soar. "

The article seemed to seek to justify the DEAland pressure on Canada. Even worse, it was loaded with statements that were contradicted by the data on the Canadian and DEAland government's own web sites. So, after waiting a few days to see if anyone would respond, I spent last Sunday afternoon writing a long letter to the editors of the National Post documenting these errors, using the two governments’ own data.

As I like to say, the best two-word explanation for cannabis prohibition is " bad journalism, " but the National Post is a really good paper and they have editorialized against prohibition.

My letter was much longer than the standard for most papers, but I included documentation so that they would know that this was not just another partisan " Ain’t so. "

Because the National Post is one of my favorite papers, I was really hoping that either my letter would spur a response or they would run a letter from someone else.

But nothing happened.

I guess I should have known better because this is hardly the first time that they have done this. In fact it was just over a year ago when they displayed a similar lapse in journalistic standards.

At that time, I did not write a letter to the editor, but this time I thought they might care, so I even waited to post my letter on MarijuanaNews.com, as I did when I wrote a letter that was promptly published by the Post's competitor, the Globe and Mail.

Oh well. It would appear that the National Post editors just don't care about the facts when the subject is cannabis. That would hardly be unique. Maybe they are afraid to think about cannabis, or maybe they can't figure out how to tell the people the truth about what is really going on.

Below is my letter to the Post and then the full text of the article in question.

I urge you to write to the editors of the National Post at

To the Editors of the National Post:

May 19, 2002

Your May 17, 2002 article " U.S. fears drug spillover from Canada Border seizures soar " by Jan Cienski and Carl Hanlon seems to seek to justify US pressure on Canadian cannabis policies by using very questionable data.

First, it sensationalizes seizure numbers by reporting them completely out of context, describing the seizures of marijuana coming into the US from Canada with terms like " dramatic increase, " " skyrocketed, " and " jumped. " Wow! Where ever will we put it all?

The problem with this is that getting large increases in small numbers is very easy. In fact, Canada is not a major supplier of cannabis to the US.

Based on seizure data, the only hard data that we have on the cannabis supply, Canadian exports amount to only about one per cent of the cannabis imported into the US from Mexico.

The recently issued RCMP Drug Situation In Canada report for 2001 has no data on such seizures, but according to the RCMP's Drug Situation In Canada 2000 report, " Though the seizures of Canadian marihuana are increasing in the US, they still total less than 3,000 kilograms which is very low compared to other types of foreign marihuana seized in the United States. "
See

For example, the May 13th Denver Rocky Mountain News reported from Laredo, Texas, that the U.S. Customs Service seized almost 3,000 kilograms of marijuana in just two incidences. That is equal to the total seizures last year at the BC-US border. Moreover, according to the US government, half of the cannabis consumed in the US is homegrown.

Then Cienski and Hanlon say that " Corporal Scott Rintoul of the RCMP estimated that 70% of the marijuana grown in Canada ends up in the United States. "

Regarding claims that

The RCMP report goes on to point out that more cannabis is seized going into Canada than coming into the US. It says, " It is interesting to note that the amount of marihuana seized in the US en route to Canada and seized in Canada after transiting the US has been in excess of 3,000 kilograms a year for a while now. "
See

That certainly does not fit the prohibitionist party line.

Next, the Cienski and Hanlon article swallows whole the prohibitionist propaganda about " BC Bud " which it tells us is " the potent form of marijuana cultivated in British Columbia hydroponic grow houses. "

Well, according to the US Department of Justice's web site, " Marijuana produced in Canada is recognized for its potency, but there is a general misconception regarding the uniqueness of this marijuana. Growers in both Canada and the United States have access to the same strains of cannabis seeds and the same cultivation technologies. Therefore, growers in both countries are capable of producing the same quality of high-grade marijuana. "
See

In fact, " BC Bud " varies greatly in quality.

Then Cienski and Hanlon say that " The potent B.C. bud, which has a THC content as high as 25%, compared to the 2% typical in the 1970s, is also leading to health concerns in the United States. "

This statement makes the basic error of comparing an average with an extreme. The data is dubious, but the comparison is absurd. One need not have any knowledge of cannabis to recognize such a fallacy.

And regarding the data, the RCMP's 1999 report, the last to mention THC averages, says "

Similarly, according to the US Department of Justice 1999 report from

This is consistent with the corresponding data from the Netherlands: " In 1997 the National Forensic Institute recorded an average THC content of 8.5% in Dutch cannabis Two studies looking at the quality of soft drugs began in late 1999. One of these studies  is measuring the THC content of the marijuana available in coffee shops on an annual basis. The results of the latter study reveal that the average THC content of Dutch-grown cannabis has not risen in recent years and now measures 8.6%, with an exceptional measurement of 25% in a single case (Trimbos Institute, 2000). "
See

Notice the distinction between the average and the extreme.

Next, Cienski and Hanlon report that " Admissions for marijuana drug treatment in Washington state now exceed the rate for treatment of alcoholism. Cannabis admissions in Cook County, Ill., have risen by 400% in the last four years. "

Then they draw a direct connection between this unexplained data and Canadian cannabis by saying, " That is causing increasing anger south of the border. One of the areas of growth has actually been through Canada, Mr. Walters told Congress recently when testifying about the U.S. drug problem. "

Blame Canada? John Walters said it, so it must be true?

Okay, but please explain how marijuana " abuse " could be a bigger social and public health problem than alcoholism in Washington state, and how it has quadrupled in Cook county in just four years, but not in the rest of the country. There is not sufficient BC Bud in Seattle or Chicago to do this, even if it were so uniquely potent.

Hint: In the US " More than half (57 percent) of marijuana admissions were referred to treatment through the criminal justice system. "
See

These were some of the 730,000 Americans who are arrested every year on marijuana possession charges, and who made deals to get " treatment " to stay out of jail. This has nothing to do with whether or not they needed treatment.

If Canada surrenders its sovereignty and continues to arrest its citizens for marijuana possession and deprive the sick and dying of medical cannabis, it won't be because of US pressure. It will be because the Canadian media accept US prohibitionist propaganda and its RCMP echoes as the unquestioned truth.

Richard Cowan
MarijuanaNews.com

The full text of the Post article from

May 17, 2002

U.S. fears drug spillover from Canada -- Border seizures soar
By Jan Cienski and Carl Hanlon, National Post, Global Television

WASHINGTON - A dramatic increase in drug seizures along the U.S.-Canadian border, coupled with an increasingly tolerant attitude in Canada toward narcotics, is fuelling U.S. concerns that Canada is becoming a source of drug problems for the United States.

If Canada does not halt what Washington perceives as a slide toward the legalization of drugs and act more vigorously to stamp out drug smuggling, the United States is prepared to retaliate by using the stick of tougher customs regulation, something which could have disastrous effects on Canada's U.S.-dependent economy.

" Canada is a sovereign country, but there are consequences when neighbours cannot co-operate on serious issues and this is a very serious issue, " said Robert Maginnis, an advisor to White House drug czar John Walters. " It appears as if it's a trend going in the wrong direction and it is incumbent on the U.S. administration and the U.S. Congress to communicate that this is a key concern. "

In recent years, U.S. authorities have been intercepting growing amounts of drugs being smuggled south from Canada, particularly the potent form of marijuana cultivated in British Columbia hydroponic grow houses known as B.C. bud.

But after border controls were tightened following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, drug seizures skyrocketed. Two years ago, the Americans seized 2,648 kilograms of marijuana coming in from British Columbia. In 2001 that figure jumped to over 3,400 kilograms. So far this year U.S. Customs has confiscated 3,100 kilograms and expects to hit 7,300 kilograms by the end of the year.

In Buffalo, N.Y., U.S. Customs has seized 350 kilograms of B.C. bud this year, three times more than last year, said Mark MacVittie, a chief inspector there.

U.S. officials attribute part of the increase to tighter border security following the Sept. 11 attacks and part to the criminal gangs which are taking over the trade and shipping drugs to the United States in larger amounts.

Corporal Scott Rintoul of the RCMP estimated that 70% of the marijuana grown in Canada ends up in the United States.

The potent B.C. bud, which has a THC content as high as 25%, compared to the 2% typical in the 1970s, is also leading to health concerns in the United States. THC is the active ingredient in marijuana.

Admissions for marijuana drug treatment in Washington state now exceed the rate for treatment of alcoholism. Cannabis admissions in Cook County, Ill., have risen by 400% in the last four years.

That is causing increasing anger south of the border. " One of the areas of growth has actually been through Canada, " Mr. Walters told Congress recently when testifying about the U.S. drug problem.

The United States is also worried that Canada could turn into a North American version of the Netherlands, attracting pot-seeking tourists and leading to pressure in surrounding countries to ease their drug laws in turn.

A recent report from the Canadian Senate that drug control was not working raised alarms in Washington, which fears it heralds a move toward legalization.

Mr. Maginnis and other administration officials are already lobbying the Canadian government to go no further on the path toward legalization. They intend to make their case at a drug policy conference next month in Quebec, where Mr. Walters is expected to make a strong argument against legalization.

The U.S. government has already helped delay Canada's medical marijuana program by refusing to supply standardized marijuana seeds from a U.S. government marijuana farm in Mississippi.

Although several states have approved medical marijuana, the federal government has blocked any attempt to find legitimate uses for the drug.
